overview:
Palau is a scatter of more than 300 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, at the far edge of Micronesia and about 900 kilometers east of the Philippines. Its total land area is only about 460 km², smaller than New York City, but its ocean territory is enormous, and most of that sea is now a protected sanctuary.

Roughly 18,000 people live in Palau, most of them on Koror island. English and Palauan are official languages, and some islands add their own. The capital, Ngerulmud, is a small hilltop complex of government buildings on the larger island of Babeldaob, making it one of the least populated capitals in the world.

Palau is a republic with an elected president, in free association with the United States. It is best known to divers as one of the finest places on Earth to see reefs, sharks and wrecks, and to scientists for protecting its waters early and firmly.
landAndNature: The Rock Islands are Palau's signature: hundreds of green limestone knobs, undercut by waves into mushroom shapes, floating in water so clear that boats seem to hover. Babeldaob, the largest island, has rivers, waterfalls and savanna as well as forest. Palau's reefs hold more than 1,300 kinds of fish and 500 kinds of coral, plus manta rays, sea turtles and the dugong. Jellyfish Lake, a saltwater lake cut off from the sea, is filled with millions of golden jellyfish that have lost most of their sting and migrate across the water each day following the sun. Saltwater crocodiles live in the mangroves, and the islands are hit by typhoons far less often than places further north.
peopleAndCulture: Palauan society traditionally traces family through the mother's line, and clan mothers choose and can remove chiefs. Villages centered on a bai, a tall meeting house with a steep thatched roof and painted storyboards along the beams telling legends; the same stories are now carved on wooden boards sold as art. Taro, tapioca, fish, fruit bats and reef fish feature in local meals. Visitors sign the Palau Pledge, stamped in their passports, promising to tread lightly on the islands. Canoe racing, baseball, which arrived with Japanese administration, and basketball are popular. The custom of bul, a chief's temporary ban on fishing a reef so it can recover, is an ancient form of conservation still respected today.
history: People reached Palau at least 3,000 years ago and built terraced hillsides and stone villages. Spain claimed the islands in the 1600s as part of its Pacific holdings, then sold them to Germany in 1899. Japan took them during World War I and ran them as part of its Pacific mandate, building towns, roads and phosphate mines. In 1944 the island of Peleliu saw one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war, and rusting tanks and plane wrecks remain. After the war Palau was administered by the United States under a United Nations trusteeship. Palauans wrote a constitution in 1979 that banned nuclear weapons from their territory, and after long negotiations Palau became independent on October 1, 1994, keeping close ties with the United States.
funFacts: Swimmers can float among millions of golden jellyfish in Palau's Jellyfish Lake, which have lost nearly all their sting.
Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary in 2009, banning shark fishing across its entire ocean territory.
Every visitor's passport is stamped with the Palau Pledge, an eco-promise written with the help of local schoolchildren.
Palau banned sunscreens containing chemicals harmful to coral reefs, one of the first countries to do so.
Ngerulmud, the capital, has only a few hundred residents and was built on a hill in the jungle in 2006.
